highlights:
# Nvidia B200 rental prices drop over 30% in less than a month

Nvidia B200 GPU rental prices have dropped over 30% in less than a month, falling to $4.22 per hour and challenging the computing power shortage narrative.

 By Mateo Mendoza 

 Published Jun 24, 2026 6:43 PM 

Cloud providers offering Nvidia B200 GPUs for artificial intelligence workloads are seeing rental rates fall sharply, signaling a shift in the high-end chip market. This price drop challenges the long-standing industry narrative that computing power remains critically scarce. Buyers and infrastructure planners now face a more competitive pricing environment than expected just weeks ago.

...

## Rental rates for Nvidia B200 GPUs have fallen sharply from May highs

The Nvidia B200 GPU serves as the centerpiece for this market adjustment. Data centers and cloud service providers utilize these chips to train large language models and execute complex artificial intelligence tasks. High demand for this hardware has spurred intense competition among suppliers seeking to secure capacity for enterprise clients.

Rental prices for the B200 have declined by more than 30 percent in less than a month. Rates peaked at 6.11 USD (around $6.11) per hour on May 30. By late June, those costs had dropped to 4.22 USD (around $4.22) per hour. This rapid decrease indicates that supply is beginning to outpace immediate demand in certain segments.

Market analysts warn that sustained price falls could undermine the argument for a persistent computing power shortage. Rich Privorotsky, a transaction platform manager, noted that increased supply directly challenges the scarcity narrative. Meanwhile, major contracts like the agreement between SpaceX and Google for 110,000 Nvidia GPUs show that long-term demand remains strong, with payments starting in October 2026.

...

Confirmed data shows that B200 rental costs have dropped significantly from their May highs. The 4.22 USD (around $4.22) rate represents the current market floor as of late June. This pricing trend provides immediate cost relief for cloud users while highlighting the dynamic nature of the artificial intelligence infrastructure market.

results.title: 算力租赁市场：从认证为王到货源为王
highlights:
算力租赁无疑是2026年A股市场最炙手可热的概念之一。在这场围绕GPU资源的争夺战中，英伟达认证资质一度被视为入场的“金牌”。国内算力租赁行业中，核心资质主要分为两大体系：英伟达合作伙伴网络（NPN）和英伟达云合作伙伴（NCP）。

...

前述分析人士对证券时报记者表示，此前，拥有上述顶级认证的民营企业可以从官方渠道直采算力卡，相比普通渠道具有显著优势。通过原厂直供可跳过中间商加价环节，拿卡成本比无核心授权的中小租赁商低30%—50%；同时货源更稳定，交付周期比普通伙伴快6—12个月，配额量多30%—50%。

2023年11月美国出口管制新规实施，上述认证沦为“摆设”。

北京腾辉智算科技有限公司CEO董春辉向证券时报记者表示，目前认证只能用于采购未受限制的产品，如英伟达的IB交换机，“实际上价值也不大了”，对拿卡没有实质帮助。

官方渠道关闭后，拿卡只能通过“桌子下面”的海外通道。据董春辉透露，H200从春节前的约230万至240万元/台，最新已涨至400万至420万元/台；B300则从约380万至400万元/台飙升至如今的900万至1000万元/台。一台搭载8颗B300 GPU的服务器在中国期货市场成交价最新已飙升至约700万元人民币。

二手设备残值同样惊人——A100新机约80万至90万元，使用两三年后仍将值80万至90万元，几乎没有折损。行业数据显示，英伟达B300按需租赁均价较2025年11月上涨超50%，Nebius已于2026年6月1日起将全系列GPU按需租赁价格全面上调。

供需关系的逆转是价格飙升的根本推手。据董春辉介绍，2025年6月成为算力市场的关键转折点——推理算力需求首次与训练算力需求持平（各占50%），此后推理份额持续高于训练。国家数据局数据显示，2025年推理数据量已达101.34艾字节，首次超过训练数据量。Token调用量呈现井喷式增长，2026年3月我国日均Token调用量突破140万亿。2024年，算力市场以训练为主，供大于求，设备大量闲置，客户违约普遍。而2025年10月以后，推理需求彻底引爆市场，算力一卡难求——连此前闲置的新疆算力都被抢空，千卡级GPU采购订单的交付周期已延长至2027年，等待时间长达12至15个月。

市场格局的剧变，让“认证壁垒”彻底失效。据董春辉分析，一线企业如利通电子、润泽科技、协创数据的真正优势已不在于认证，而在于“入局早”——早期手里握有万卡订单、有实际交付案例和“办卡”经验。目前大家处于同一起跑线——拿货资源重新洗牌，谁有渠道拿到卡、搞定资金、实现闭环，谁就有竞争力。

跨界者的动机不难理解——算力项目金额巨大，一个万卡订单可能就能赶上公司过去多年营收总和。但董春辉指出，与2024年初的纯概念炒作不同，现在大部分公司确实与自身经营有关，能否成功取决于公司基因——是否有客户积累、是否专业。算力租赁项目闭环需要四个基本要素：客户端拿到真实订单、供应链端拿到货源、资金端解决投入难题，以及具备运营端GPU卡集群调优的能力。

...

不过，算力租赁也是一门重资产、长周期的生意。在高杠杆、高折旧的双重压力下，资金链的稳健与资产运营效率，将是这场算力淘金战中决定生死的关键变量。

results.title: 计算机：英伟达B200租赁价格大幅提升 算力紧缺态势或将延续__新浪财经_新浪网
highlights:
# 计算机：英伟达B200租赁价格大幅提升 算力紧缺态势或将延续

 类别：行业 机构：长江证券股份有限公司 研究员：杨洋/郭敬超/陈耀文 日期：2026-06-24 

 事件描述 6 月17 日，AI 推理基础设施服务商Baseten 首席执行官Tuhin Srivastava 透露，其云服务商已于今年5 月提前通知，英伟达B200 GPU 的每小时租赁单价将在10 月合同续约时，从现行的2.63 美元涨至5.10 美元，涨幅约94%。 事件评论 涨价已蔓延至H100，算力成本或将持续上涨。我们关注到，除英伟达B200 等高端GPU的算力租赁价格上涨外，H100 等上一代GPU 的算力租赁价格也呈现上涨趋势。根据SemiAnalysis 数据，H100 GPU 一年期租约合同价格已从2025 年10 月的低点每小时每GPU 1.70 美元大幅上涨至2026 年3 月的2.35 美元，涨幅接近40%。同时，所有种类的GPU 按需租赁的容量也已经售罄，这或说明算力涨价已具备一定普遍性，算力使用成本或将持续上涨。 供给端紧张态势延续背景下，算力涨价趋势或将持续。在海外算力租赁涨价的同时，我们关注到，今年以来国内腾讯云及阿里云已经由于供应链成本上涨而上调AI 算力相关产品价格，最高涨幅达34%。国内外云服务商提前数月主动通知涨价或已表明在算力持续紧缺的背景下，算力租赁行业已由买方市场转向卖方市场。同时，当前GPU 交付也存在瓶颈，据Tuhin Srivastava 介绍，当前采购1000 块GPU 的交付排期已普遍延至明年第二季度，等待周期长达12 至15 个月，短期内难以通过采购途径补足算力缺口，算力供需失衡格局或将进一步加剧，算力涨价趋势在短期内或难以改变。 Agent 时代来临，算力消耗或将持续提升。2026 年6 月1 日，英伟达创始人兼CEO 黄仁勋在台北GTC 大会发表主题演讲，并宣告Agentic AI 时代全面到来。随着ClaudeCode，以及开源agent 框架Open Claw 等工具的逐步普及，人们正逐步改变使用软件的方式。AI 也逐步由"生成式"转向"代理式"，其核心特征在于通过自主决策、环境感知与任务执行能力，实现从“被动响应”到“主动服务”的跨越。巴克莱预测，当前市场对AI 训练与推理所需的GPU 及定制芯片数量的预估可能严重偏低。预计到2025 年，实际需求量将较现有预期高出约250%；而到2027 年，这一数字更可能飙升至原先预期的14 倍。 我们认为，随着AI 智能体的应用范围进一步拓展，算力需求有望持续扩张。 算力租赁价格持续提升，关注算力产业投资机遇。在当前算力需求大幅提升且供给端持续紧张的背景下，算力涨价趋势或仍将持续，进而传导至算力产业链，惠及相关公司。建议关注：1）国产算力产业链，重点关注国产算力龙头：寒武纪、海光信息；2）云服务商；3）算力供应商。 风险提示 1、AI 产业发展不及预期； 2、技术迭代与设备折旧过快的风险。

results.title: There's been a halt in the market and it's being read incorrectly. | Nicolas El-Joukhadar
highlights:
There's been a halt in the market and it's being read incorrectly.

Commentators are looking at the indices, seeing h100 rentals down 10 to 20 percent, and calling the top. They're ignoring that contract pricing is still up around 30 percent YTD.

The halt I'm referring to is in available capacity.

From what I can see, demand is still greater than supply. I know what is live today and what comes live soon. Right now I am not seeing any uncontracted live capacity at meaningful scale. Nothing past 64 nodes. Nor am I seeing any uncontracted capacity coming live in the next 8 weeks.

The earliest delivery I can point to is October. Customers are still asking for August.

So an honest question.

Is anyone seeing real uncontracted capacity land in the next 8 weeks?
Real meaning a contracted data center and orders placed. Not the usual 6 weeks to deliver with no DC and no hardware ordered.

results.title: 英伟达芯片遇冷！B200算力租赁价格大跌超30%_新浪科技_新浪网
highlights:
2026年06月24日 12:39 快科技 

快科技6月24日消息，据媒体报道，AI芯片的定价权，正在经历微妙而关键的转变。据预测平台Kalshi的交易员观察，英伟达AI芯片的市场议价能力已出现下滑迹象。

作为支撑超大规模数据中心运转的核心中枢，英伟达B200芯片的租赁价格近期持续走低。根据实时GPU算力价格数据平台Ornn的统计，B200的每小时租赁价格在5月30日攀升至6.11美元，创下近三个月来的最高点。

然而自那以后，价格便一路下行，截至上周末已跌至4.22美元，短短不到一个月内跌幅高达31%。

在AI圈，算力被比作“新时代的石油”，GPU被视为炼油厂，而英伟达则被等同于沙特阿美。

然而，这一“定价权神话”正面临现实挑战。高盛One-Delta交易台主管Rich Privorotsky上周发出警告：“如果供应增加且租赁价格持续走低，这将直接挑战‘算力资源短缺’这一核心论调。”

当然，目前仍有部分市场人士相对乐观。本月早些时候，SpaceX和谷歌刚刚达成云服务协议。

根据该协议，谷歌同意从2026年10月到2029年6月每月向SpaceX支付9.2亿美元。SpaceX提供的算力包括11万块英伟达GPU、CPU以及内存。

results.title: 輝達 AI 晶片在陸黑市價飆 DGX B300 伺服器售價半年翻倍 | 大陸政經 | 兩岸 | 經濟日報
highlights:
頂級輝達AI晶片在中國黑市的價格今年來上漲逾倍。（路透） 

2026/06/25 02:25:58

 經濟日報 編譯任中原、陳苓／綜合外電 

 雖然美國限制先進晶片輸往中國大陸，但陸企對輝達的AI晶片，需求依舊強勁，這些晶片在中國黑市價格已經大漲一倍以上。

 英國金融時報（FT）訪問多位中國大陸晶片交易商，發現輝達旗艦DGX B300伺服器，過去半年價格從人民幣400萬元漲到人民幣800萬元以上（約新台幣3,744萬元）。這款伺服器內含八顆Blackwell繪圖處理器（GPU），美國市場零售價約40萬美元。

 交易商並說，輝達RTX 6000 Pro工作站晶片，售價也由年初時約人民幣5萬元漲到人民幣13萬元（約新台幣61萬元）。RTX6000是新創業者開發大型語言模型常用的晶片，RTX 6000和DGX B300均受華府管制，禁止出口至中國。

 輝達晶片在大陸黑市的價格大漲，顯示美國最新的出口管制，壓縮黑市取得晶片的途徑，也顯示儘管北京當局力推以國產品取代輝達，當地對輝達處理器的需求仍然強勁。

 貿易商表示：「交易漏洞已縮小，價格飆漲也讓中間商的交易風險日益攀升」。交易商指出，去年底美國當局加強調查非法晶片出口後，供應遭受嚴重破壞。

 台灣及馬來西亞主管機關也開始調查晶片走私，設法阻撓晶片轉往中國大陸。賣家表示，這些加強監管行動已使他們更難取得輝達晶片。而中國當局也加強監管輝達產品進口，包括H20及H200晶片，促使國內業者加速採用華為等生產的替代品。有交易商指出，H200原本在中國的供應量相對較多，供給受限後大幅加劇市場短缺。

 多位交易商透露，有鑒於此，中國客戶採購的輝達硬體日益多元，包括能改用於AI運算的遊戲處理器、舊款資料中心設備如A100晶片等，好繞過限制。一位交易商說：「A100存貨很快就賣光了，企業別無選擇，只能買舊貨」。內建A100晶片的伺服器，價格從去年底約人民幣20萬元漲到人民幣60萬元。

 輝達晶片供給吃緊，推升了中國AI算力的租賃成本。兩年前當地的GPU租賃價格普遍低於美國，反映輝達晶片走私猖獗。如今美中的大型雲端和GPU租賃平台價格相當；而且倘若平台主要採用輝達最新的Blackwell晶片，價格還高於美國。

results.title: Nvidia AI kit gets costly behind China’s walls – Fudzilla.com
highlights:
China’s smugglers are charging silly money for Nvidia AI kit as Washington squeezes the chip back channels.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia’s AI chips have more than doubled in price on China’s black market, as US export controls collide with stubborn Chinese demand.

Its DGX B300 server has climbed to more than Rmb8mn, about €1.03mn, during the past six months, up from Rmb4mn, about €517,000.

The eight-Blackwell GPU box normally sells in the US for about $400,000, which makes the China markup look properly bonkers. Nvidia’s RTX 6000 Pro workstation chip, popular with start-ups running large language models, has risen from about Rmb50,000, about €6,500, to as much as Rmb130,000, about €16,800.

The RTX 6000 and DGX B300 are barred from export to China, which has given the grey market a lovely excuse to empty wallets.

“The loopholes have shrunk. It is becoming more and more risky for intermediaries to trade these chips as prices have surged,” said one trader who sells to large data centre clients.

...

Chinese authorities have tightened scrutiny of Nvidia products, including the H20 and H200, as Beijing pushes Huawei and other local alternatives. Huawei has released its Ascend 950PR AI processor, but traders said Chinese buyers are still snapping up Nvidia gaming processors and older A100 accelerators.

“Stocks of A100s are selling out very quickly. Companies don’t have a choice but to buy the old ones,” one trader told the FT.

Servers using A100 chips have jumped from about Rmb200,000, about €25,900, late last year to as much as Rmb600,000, about €77,600.

...

“No one dares to do this at scale. You can go against the American rules, but not the Chinese,” said one trader.

The squeeze has pushed up GPU rental prices in China, which now match or beat US levels for some Blackwell-based systems.

“Prices of all products have skyrocketed. Many people have reduced their demand at these prices. It’s been a difficult year,” one seller said.

results.title: The Fix for AI Bottlenecks: A 'CPU Renaissance' Arrives - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights:
The CPU is rising again. Since the ChatGPT moment in 2022, the protagonist of AI infrastructure has unquestionably been the GPU. Whether for foundation models or services, creating AI required securing GPUs first. AI model developers such as Google and OpenAI, as well as global conglomerates and startups seeking to internalize AI technology, all jumped into the battle to secure GPUs. GPU demand exploded, and an asymmetry of insufficient supply persisted for some time.

...

When the priority is to create a usable AI model—in other words, when AI training matters—the GPU is in the spotlight. The GPU is designed to execute complex computations in parallel and pursue efficient work. The GPU is essential when performing large volumes of identical commands simultaneously. The same is true for AI model training. Because rapidly training large volumes of data is important, parallel computation is needed, and the GPU has been put to good use here. Yoo Eung-jun, CEO of June AI Consulting and former head of Nvidia Korea, explained, "In the AI training stage, parallel computation that processes hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of pieces of data simultaneously is important," adding, "Data center GPUs are equipped with thousands of computing cores, optimized for AI training."

...

tower,

...

The problem is that the control tower's performance falls short of the AI industry's expectations. The GPU resources stationed in data centers must be operated as efficiently as possible, but the CPU's control speed cannot keep pace with the countless work commands. The CPU has begun to be pointed to as a cause of the AI bottleneck. Lee Yong-hyuk, CTO of Klusch, an AI infrastructure platform company, noted, "To use an analogy, the AI bottleneck is a situation where GPUs sit idle because they cannot receive work," pointing out, "Delays in CPU data pre-processing, inefficient GPU task distribution, and the narrow bandwidth of the passage (interconnect) between the CPU and GPU correspond to the AI bottleneck."

...

Behind the ignition of Big Tech's CPU competition also lies concern over AI data center operating costs. The longer the AI bottleneck lasts, the more AI companies not only fall behind in AI development speed but also have to bear expensive data center electricity bills in the meantime. They end up failing to produce results while only draining costs. Accordingly, the common view in the industry is that for some time, general-purpose CPUs from Intel and AMD and Big Tech companies' proprietary CPUs will coexist in AI data centers.

CEO Yoo emphasized, "Electricity bills account for 30 to 40 percent of data center operating costs," adding, "Just as Nvidia and Amazon Web Services (AWS) adopted Arm-based designs when developing CPUs for their overwhelming energy efficiency, CPU competitiveness leads directly to cost competitiveness." CTO Park said, "Going forward, global Big Tech companies will focus on the performance and power efficiency of the entire system that combines CPU, GPU, memory, and network."

results.title: A Megawatt Is Not a Megawatt Anymore - by Clarice Qiu
highlights:
But this is not just a bearish story about power shortage. It is also not a simple story about overbuilding.

The next cycle is more interesting than that.

It is a sorting event.

The market can be short and oversupplied at the same time.

Short deployable AI capacity. Short high-density power. Short liquid-cooled space. Short interconnection positions. Short fuel-cell manufacturing capacity. Short gas transport in the markets where everyone wants to build. Short platforms that can route workloads to the right compute at the right price.

But long generic capacity. Long announcements. Long powered-shell promises. Long commodity GPU rental. Long sites that looked scarce back when everyone assumed power was just an input.

The valuable product is no longer simply the building.

It is not even the megawatt.

It is the usable, deployable, workload-matched megawatt — delivered before the customer’s demand curve moves somewhere else.

And increasingly, it is the ability to turn that megawatt into useful compute.

The Oversupply Question Everyone Is Asking Wrong

The obvious question is: when do AI data centers hit oversupply?

The answer is probably 2027 to 2029.

But not in the way people picture it.

It will not look like empty buildings everywhere. It will look like a sorting event.

Goldman Sachs Research expects U.S. data center power demand to climb from roughly 31 GW in 2025 to 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW in 2027. JLL projects roughly 100 GW of new capacity globally between 2026 and 2030. CBRE reported record North American net absorption in 2025.

So the near-term market is not loose. It is still tight.

But cycles do not break at the moment everyone is short.

They break when capital committed during the shortage arrives into a market that has changed.

That is the setup now. The projects financed during the 2024–2026 AI panic begin arriving in the 2027–2029 window.

Some will be exactly what the market needs: high-density, liquid-cooled, power-secure, well-located, with creditworthy tenants and flexible workload design.

Some will not.

The market will not ask:

“How many megawatts did you announce?”

It will ask:

Can those megawatts actually run the workload customers need, when they need it, at economics that still make sense?

That is a far more brutal test.

And it is how you get oversupply inside a shortage.

...

This does not mean every hyperscaler project works. It means the model is evolving from cloud infrastructure into cloud-plus-energy infrastructure — a much larger and more complex business.

4. GPU Cloud and Neocloud: From GPU Landlord to Compute Liquidity Layer

This is the model people most easily misunderstand.

The bearish version is simple: GPU clouds finance expensive hardware, fight depreciation, depend on utilization, and sit inside long power cycles they do not fully control.

All true.

But that is not the whole story.

The better GPU clouds are not merely renting GPUs by the hour. They are becoming compute liquidity providers.

They absorb demand that hyperscalers cannot serve quickly. They support startups that need capacity before they can sign enterprise-scale cloud commitments. They route workloads across training, fine-tuning, evaluation, synthetic data generation, batch inference, and burst demand.

The weak version of this model is commodity bare-metal rental.

That business compresses as supply improves, older GPUs reprice, and customers become more sophisticated.

The strong version is workload matching: the ability to put the right job on the right GPU, in the right location, at the right price, with enough reliability that customers do not have to think about the underlying infrastructure.

A B200 in a high-density liquid-cooled cluster, an H100 in a regional neocloud, an A100 in a private enterprise cluster, and a lower-cost decentralized GPU are not the same product.

But they can all be valuable if matched to the right workload.

The operator that can price, schedule, package, and guarantee those differences becomes more valuable, not less.

The next GPU cloud winner may not be the one with the most GPUs.

...

Decentralized GPU cloud is easiest to dismiss when it is pitched as a replacement for hyperscale training clusters.

That is the wrong comparison.

Frontier training still wants dense, high-bandwidth, highly reliable clusters. Decentralized networks are not naturally built for that.

Their better role is different:

They are the overflow valve for the AI compute market.

Inference, rendering, batch processing, synthetic data generation, evaluation runs, fine-tuning jobs, and latency-tolerant workloads do not all need the most expensive GPU in the most power-constrained data center.

Some need price.

Some need availability.

Some need geography.

Some need burst capacity for a few hours.

Some simply need to run somewhere that is good enough.

That is where decentralized GPU cloud becomes interesting.

Its problem is not demand. Its problem is trust, scheduling, reliability, verification, and enterprise procurement.

...

When Does the Glut Arrive?

The glut arrives when the market stops treating all megawatts as equal.

That could begin as early as 2027, become visible through 2028 and 2029 — and it will not be a single national oversupply event.

It will be segmented.

Short: high-density, liquid-cooled, power-secure capacity in the right markets. Long: generic shells, delayed campuses, stranded sites, capacity built for the wrong workload mix.

Short: operators with firm power, flexible architecture, and creditworthy customers. Long: operators with announcements, land positions, and optimistic energization assumptions.

Short: deployable capacity. Long: theoretical capacity.

Short: GPU clouds with utilization, orchestration, and differentiated customer access. Long: undifferentiated GPU rental with weak workload stickiness.

Short: decentralized GPU networks that solve trust and scheduling. Long: networks that only aggregate supply without making it usable.

The cycle will not be judged by who announced the most megawatts.

It will be judged by who converts power and GPUs into useful work.

Honest Caveats

Several things deserve naming explicitly.

The AI cloud revenue figures behind the off-grid math — SemiAnalysis estimates in the range of $10–12 million per megawatt per year — are estimates, not audited financials, and they reflect premium AI workloads. General-purpose compute, lower utilization, or declining GPU rental rates would change the economics materially.

The xAI lawsuit remains unresolved; the legal outcome should not be prejudged. The relevant point is the regulatory signal, not a verdict.

The alternative power stack is not guaranteed to scale smoothly. ... This piece argues the bottleneck migrates — not that any single workaround solves the whole problem.

The GPU cloud opportunity is real, but not every GPU cloud becomes a platform. Some remain commodity hardware rental businesses, more exposed to utilization swings, depreciation, and price compression.

The decentralized GPU cloud opportunity is also real, but it depends on execution. Trust, reliability, scheduling, verification, and enterprise procurement are not footnotes. They are the product.

And the transition will be uneven. Legacy enterprise colo, AI training campuses, inference-heavy edge deployments, sovereign AI infrastructure, and decentralized compute networks will not face the same density, latency, or uptime requirements.

“Oversupply” and “shortage” can be true in different segments of the same market on the same day.

results.title: Nvidia's B300 Systems Fetch Over $1 Million On China's Underground Market - Dataconomy
highlights:
Prices of Nvidia’s restricted AI chips have more than doubled on China’s black market over the past six months, according to the Financial Times. The DGX B300 server, which contains eight B300 GPUs, has surged to over 8 million yuan (approximately $1.1 million) in China’s underground market, up from about 4 million yuan late last year. In comparison, the same system retails for around $550,000 in the United States.

China’s customs authorities began blocking imports of Nvidia’s H200 chips in January, with directives stating that the processors were “not permitted” to enter the country. Concurrently, Beijing has pressured domestic companies to limit purchases of foreign hardware, permitting exceptions only for university research.

...

The strong demand for Nvidia hardware persists among Chinese enterprises despite Beijing’s attempts to shift reliance to domestic alternatives from Huawei and local chipmakers. The crackdown on grey-market smuggling, intensified by the arrest of a Supermicro co-founder earlier this year, has sharply reduced supply without affecting demand.

Reuters reported in April that monthly rental prices for B300 servers in China reached as high as 190,000 yuan, demonstrating the severe compute scarcity faced by Chinese AI firms. Meanwhile, Nvidia shares fell more than 4% to around $200, extending a decline of nearly 3% over the past month, amid broader technology selloffs and concerns about its revenue from China.

Nvidia has not generated significant revenue from H200 sales to China, despite having U.S. government export license approvals. The company expressed uncertainty in May regarding whether any imports would ultimately be allowed.
